newsitem.title: INDIA: Joyous welcome planned for new Kashmir leader.
newsitem.headline: Joyous welcome planned for new Kashmir leader.

text.p: National Conference party chief Farooq Abdullah returns to a hero's welcome in Srinagar on Saturday after a landslide poll victory and will seek to defuse separatist tension, party officials said.

Early this week, the National Conference swept 57 of the 87 assembly seats in India's northern Jammu and Kashmir state in the first local polls since a separatist revolt broke out in 1990, killing more than 20,000 people in the last seven years.

"Dr Abdullah will receive a rousing reception from senior National Conference members," party spokesman Saifuddin Soz told Reuters. Other members of the largest pro-India party in Kashmir said 5,000 cadres would turn out to receive Abdullah at Srinagar's airport.
A conclave of senior members would later formally elect Abdullah as the leader of their legislative party on Sunday, they said. He is expected to be sworn in as chief minister next Tuesday.

Abdullah will not have much time for celebrations. One of his first tasks will be to deal with thorny separatist sentiment. Dozens of separatist groups fighting for freedom or closer ties to neighbouring Pakistan have already rejected Abdullah's government.
The separatists, who boycotted the polls, calling them a mockery of the Kashmiri people's aspirations, have also rebuffed a peace overture Abdullah made early this week.
Abdullah told Reuters in an interview in the Indian capital on Wednesday that he was ready to hold talks with the separatist leaders, but would deal with the militants with a firm hand.
On Friday the All- Parties' Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, which includes some 30 separatist groups, rejected the offer.
"We outright reject this offer," Gulam Nabi Sumji, a Hurriyat leader told reporters in the state's summer capital, Srinagar.
"How can we talk to Farooq Abdullah, who is at the mercy of New Delhi?" Sumji said. "Abdullah's government will be a puppet regime of the Indian government."
He said the Hurriyat would continue its fight for self-determination for Kashmiris. "We will continue our freedom struggle till it reaches its logical end," Sumji added.

"The doors are still open for all people, including the Hurriyat," spokesman Soz told Reuters. "We want dialogue with everybody because dialogue is the only process by which we can achieve peace in the region."
The spokesman said his party would continue to wait for the Hurriyat to agree to talks.
Abdullah has said he would like his party to join Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition in New Delhi.
The National Conference campaigned on a demand for more autonomy for the Himalayan state.
India's constitution gives the state control over all matters except foreign relations, defence and communications. Since 1952, the federal government has gradually claimed some of the power.
